newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain cabinet meets, set to approve 1997 budget.
newsitem.headline: Spain cabinet meets, set to approve 1997 budget.

text.p: The Spanish cabinet is set to approve the government's 1997 budget draft on Friday, and financial markets raced ahead in expectation of austere accounts that would whip Spain into shape for Europe's common currency.

At a press conference following approval, Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato is expected to release the grand framework of the budget, although details on spending items are likely to be withheld until the draft is presented to parliament on Monday.
A spokesman for the Economy Ministry said Rato would release a limited table of the economic forecasts underlying the 1997 accounts and give a brief news conference.
All further information would be made available at a more detailed news conference on Monday at 0730 GMT, he said.
The government has pledged to cut the deficit to three percent of gross domestic product in 1997 from the 4.4 percent projected for this year.
The government has said it expects income to rise six percent in 1997, and plans to cap spending growth at around two percent - well beneath the 2.6 percent inflation rate projected.
Even so, the government must slash 800 billion pesetas in spending from the accounts.
Spanish financial markets have become convinced the government will deliver on its pledge.

The stock market has risen to 4,203.48 from 4025.47 at the end of August. Spanish bond futures prices have soared more than six full points this month, while yields on the 10-year benchmark bond have dropped sixty basis points.
The peseta continued to strengthen amid market conviction Bank of Spain sales were the only thing holding it back.
The budget is expected to slash 1.2 trillion pesetas ($9.41 billion) from the public deficit.
The ruling Popular Party minority government will submit the draft to parliament for approval on Monday after securing the support of several smaller parties this week.

The government has vowed to cut the deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) from 4.4 percent in 1996, meeting the target for convergence set out in the Maastricht Treaty on European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

The government is counting on a 6.0 percent rise in receipts while spending should be capped at around 2.0 percent, 0.6 percent below the forecast rate of inflation for 1997. The government also plans to freeze public salaries.
